subject: Cognitive Science
title: Thinking Fast and Slow
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Thinking Fast and Slow.

hook.text: What's 2 + 2? Instant. What's 17 × 24? You slow down. Two systems, two speeds, two kinds of thinking.

buildup.text: Kahneman's System 1 is fast, automatic, and intuitive. System 2 is slow, deliberate, and effortful.

discovery.text: System 1 handles most decisions, freeing System 2 for complex ones. But System 1 makes predictable errors.

twist.text: System 2 is lazy. It often endorses System 1's snap judgment instead of checking it.

climax.text: Most cognitive biases are System 1 errors that System 2 fails to catch. Awareness helps, but not much.

punchline.text: Your fast brain decides. Your slow brain justifies.

quiz.question: What is the role of System 1 in decision-making?
options: Fast, automatic processing of most decisions
Slow, careful analysis of all problems

details.summary: Daniel Kahneman divided thinking into System 1, fast and intuitive, and System 2, slow and deliberate. System 1 handles routine decisions automatically. System 2 engages for complex reasoning but is lazy and often defers to System 1, which introduces systematic biases.
details.whyItMatters: The dual-process framework is the most influential idea in modern cognitive science. It explains why smart people consistently make predictable reasoning errors.
takeaways: System 1 is fast, automatic, and always running
System 2 is slow, effortful, and easily depleted
Most biases arise from System 1 shortcuts going unchecked

faq.question: Can you train System 2 to override System 1?
faq.answer: To a limited degree. You can learn to recognize situations where System 1 is likely to err and deliberately engage System 2. But System 2 is resource-limited and cannot monitor everything. The practical approach is building environments and checklists that prevent predictable System 1 errors.

faq.question: Is System 1 always wrong and System 2 always right?
faq.answer: Not at all. System 1 is right most of the time and is essential for efficient functioning. Experts develop accurate System 1 intuitions through experience. System 2 can also reach wrong conclusions through flawed reasoning. The key is knowing when each system is reliable.
